---
title: "wfmR Academic Demo"
subtitle: "Formal figure captions and notes"
author: "Will Mackey"
brand: "_extensions/wfmr-academic/_brand.yml"
bibliography: references.bib
abstract: |
  This demo shows the academic article defaults in `wfmR`: a title page with an
  abstract, an author affiliation and footnote, formal chart and table captions,
  smaller subtitle/notes/source blocks, and floats that stay close to their
  references. The examples use ggplot2 [@wickham2016ggplot2], standard
  principles for statistical graphics [@cleveland1993visualizing;
  @tufte2001visual], and built-in R datasets so that the document can be
  rendered without external data files.
format:
  wfmr-academic-html:
    toc: true
    toc-depth: 2
    fig-format: svg
    mainfont: "Newsreader, Georgia, Cambria, Iowan Old Style, Palatino Linotype, Palatino, serif"
    linestretch: 1.58
    embed-resources: true
    code-fold: false
    code-tools: false
  wfmr-academic-pdf:
    toc: false
    fig-pos: tb
    include-in-header:
      text: |
        \wfmAcademicAuthor{Will Mackey}{Australian National University}{This is a demonstration author note for the academic PDF title page.}
execute:
  warning: false
  message: false
  echo: false
crossref:
  fig-title: Chart
  fig-prefix: Chart
---

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
library(wfmR)
library(ggplot2)
wfm_chart_defaults(style = "academic")

mtcars_cyl <- transform(mtcars, cyl = factor(cyl), gear = factor(gear))

wide_vehicle_table <- data.frame(
  Model = row.names(mtcars),
  Cylinders = mtcars$cyl,
  Gears = mtcars$gear,
  Transmission = ifelse(mtcars$am == 1, "Manual", "Automatic"),
  `Miles per gallon` = sprintf("%.1f", mtcars$mpg),
  `Weight (1000 lbs)` = sprintf("%.2f", mtcars$wt),
  `Gross horsepower` = mtcars$hp,
  `Quarter-mile time` = sprintf("%.2f", mtcars$qsec),
  `Rear axle ratio` = sprintf("%.2f", mtcars$drat),
  Displacement = sprintf("%.0f", mtcars$disp),
  check.names = FALSE
)
wide_vehicle_table <- wide_vehicle_table[
  order(wide_vehicle_table$Cylinders, wide_vehicle_table$Gears, wide_vehicle_table$Model),
]
row.names(wide_vehicle_table) <- NULL

category_df <- data.frame(
  group = factor(
    tools::toTitleCase(names(wfm_palette())),
    levels = tools::toTitleCase(names(wfm_palette()))
  ),
  value = c(31, 27, 24, 21, 18, 16, 13)
)

air_df <- data.frame(
  year = floor(as.numeric(time(AirPassengers))),
  month = factor(month.abb[cycle(AirPassengers)], levels = month.abb),
  passengers = as.numeric(AirPassengers)
)

wfm_demo_table <- function(
  x,
  caption,
  label,
  align = NULL,
  col.names = NULL,
  subtitle = NULL,
  notes = NULL,
  source = NULL,
  latex_resize = FALSE
) {
  sentence <- function(value) {
    if (is.null(value) || value == "") {
      return(character())
    }
    if (grepl("[.!?]$", value)) value else paste0(value, ".")
  }
  details <- paste(
    c(sentence(subtitle), sentence(notes), sentence(source)),
    collapse = " "
  )
  note_html <- if (nzchar(details)) {
    paste0("\n<div class=\"chart-notes figure-notes\"><p>", details, "</p></div>\n")
  } else {
    ""
  }
  note_latex <- if (nzchar(details)) {
    paste0(
      "\n\\par\\nopagebreak[4]\\vspace{0.35em}",
      "\\begingroup\\raggedright\\footnotesize\\linespread{0.92}\\selectfont{}",
      details,
      "\\par\\endgroup\n"
    )
  } else {
    ""
  }

  if (knitr::is_latex_output()) {
    body <- knitr::kable(
      x,
      format = "latex",
      booktabs = TRUE,
      align = align,
      col.names = col.names,
      row.names = FALSE
    )
    if (isTRUE(latex_resize)) {
      body <- paste0("\\resizebox{\\textwidth}{!}{%\n", body, "\n}")
    }
    cat(body, note_latex, sep = "\n")
    return(invisible(NULL))
  }

  body <- knitr::kable(x, align = align, col.names = col.names, row.names = FALSE)
  knitr::asis_output(paste0(body, note_html))
}
```

# Descriptive Evidence

@fig-academic-boxplot provides a basic descriptive view of fuel economy by
cylinder count. This section is intentionally long enough to test whether floats
move to the top or bottom of nearby pages without separating images, captions,
notes, and sources. In an applied paper, this is the common case: a paragraph
introduces the object, the object appears near the reference, and the reader can
understand the chart without searching elsewhere for metadata.

The academic style differs from the report style in two important ways. First,
figure captions sit below the image, while table captions sit above the table.
Second, the subtitle, notes, and source are kept in a smaller details block that
travels with the float. The layout is deliberately plain: the caption label is
centred, the caption text is not bold, and the surrounding prose remains in the
normal article text block.

The prose also uses ordinary cross-references throughout. This matters for PDF
testing because the reference to @fig-academic-boxplot appears before the
figure itself. If LaTeX has to move the chart, the float should still land close
to the first reference while preserving the title, image, subtitle, notes, and
source as one grouped object. The same rule is checked later by one wide table
that is large enough to make the placement decision visible.

The next paragraph is dummy placement text. It is intentionally plain and
repetitive so the figure is not trivially placed where it appears in the source.
The reference has already appeared, and the chart should now be eligible for the
top or bottom of the nearest page depending on available space. A manuscript
paragraph in this position would usually describe data construction, sample
restrictions, or the intuition behind the descriptive comparison.

A second dummy paragraph lengthens the gap before the first figure. The aim is
to make the contact sheet reveal whether LaTeX is managing a float queue or
whether the object is being pinned inline. The grouped caption, image, subtitle,
notes, and source should move together.

```{r}
#| label: fig-academic-boxplot
#| chart-title: "Fuel economy differs by cylinder count"
#| chart-subtitle: "A simple example using the built-in mtcars data"
#| chart-notes: "Boxes show the interquartile range and median. Whiskers use ggplot2 defaults."
#| chart-source: "R datasets package."
#| fig-width: 6.6
#| fig-height: 4.2
mtcars_cyl |>
  ggplot(aes(cyl, mpg, fill = cyl)) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.62, alpha = 0.9) +
  scale_fill_wfm() +
  scale_y_wfm() +
  labs(x = "Cylinders", y = NULL, subtitle = "Miles per gallon") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

# Bivariate Pattern

@fig-academic-scatter uses a scatter plot with a fitted line. It checks
that a chart with a legend, a subtitle-style y-axis label, and a formal caption
still feels coherent when it appears inside the academic PDF format. The example
follows the same broad grammar-of-graphics logic as @wilkinson2005grammar:
variables are mapped to position and colour, the fitted line is a separate
layer, and the scale choices remain part of the theme rather than the
substantive claim.

Dummy placement prose continues here. The next chart is referenced early in the
section, but the source object appears only after this paragraph. If top/bottom
floating is working, the chart should not carve out a mid-page slot simply
because the code chunk is written here.

The additional text keeps the scatter plot from landing trivially in source
order. A real empirical paper would use this space to explain identification,
measurement, or modelling choices; the demo uses it to make page composition
visible.

```{r}
#| label: fig-academic-scatter
#| chart-title: "Fuel economy declines with vehicle weight"
#| chart-subtitle: "Points are grouped by cylinder count"
#| chart-notes: "The fitted line is an ordinary least squares fit shown for visual orientation."
#| chart-source: "R datasets package."
#| fig-width: 6.6
#| fig-height: 4.2
mtcars_cyl |>
  ggplot(aes(wt, mpg, colour = cyl)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.4, alpha = 0.88) +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "lm",
    formula = y ~ x,
    se = FALSE,
    colour = "#2F2F33",
    linewidth = 0.6
  ) +
  scale_colour_wfm(name = "Cylinders") +
  scale_y_wfm() +
  labs(
    x = "Weight (1,000 lbs)",
    y = NULL,
    subtitle = "Miles per gallon"
  )
```

# Distributional Checks

@fig-academic-density and @tbl-academic-wide-vehicles add two more object types
before the palette stress test. The density chart checks overlapping
semi-transparent fills and a legend, while the table is deliberately wide enough
to exercise caption placement, PDF scaling, and table float behaviour in one
object.

This is a useful applied-paper stress test because distributional plots often
sit in the narrative before model results, and wide descriptive tables often
appear as supporting evidence. The visual design should therefore stay
disciplined even when several labelled objects occur within a short span of
prose [@cleveland1993visualizing].

Dummy placement text makes this section behave more like a manuscript page than
a gallery. The chart has already been referenced, but the source chunk is still
below this paragraph. LaTeX should be free to decide whether the density chart
belongs at the bottom of the current page or at the top of the next.

The wide table is deliberately introduced in the same narrative block. That
creates pressure on the float queue and makes it easier to see whether tables
are genuine floats. If the table appears mid-page because it is a `longtable`,
the test has failed.

```{r}
#| label: fig-academic-density
#| chart-title: "Fuel-economy distributions differ by cylinder count"
#| chart-subtitle: "Density curves provide a crowded legend example"
#| chart-notes: "The curves are illustrative and use the small built-in mtcars data."
#| chart-source: "R datasets package."
#| fig-width: 6.6
#| fig-height: 4.0
mtcars_cyl |>
  ggplot(aes(mpg, fill = cyl, colour = cyl)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.32, linewidth = 0.7) +
  scale_fill_wfm(name = "Cylinders") +
  scale_colour_wfm(name = "Cylinders") +
  scale_y_wfm() +
  labs(x = "Miles per gallon", y = NULL, subtitle = "Density")
```

@tbl-academic-wide-vehicles should inherit the formal table caption treatment,
with the caption above the table and the small details below. This is also a
quick check that shaded HTML rows remain subtle while the PDF table keeps the
plain academic appearance.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-academic-wide-vehicles
#| tbl-cap: "Wide vehicle summary."
#| results: asis
wfm_demo_table(
  wide_vehicle_table,
  caption = "Wide vehicle summary.",
  label = "tbl-academic-wide-vehicles",
  align = c("l", "r", "r", "l", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r"),
  subtitle = "Selected car-level measures from the built-in mtcars data",
  notes = "The table is intentionally wide and uses all 32 cars so that PDF placement and scaling remain visible.",
  source = "R datasets package.",
  latex_resize = TRUE
)
```

# Time-Series Example

@fig-academic-air uses the built-in `AirPassengers` series to test a different
data shape. The figure is a line chart rather than a categorical comparison,
which gives the PDF output another opportunity to place a figure at the top or
bottom of a nearby page while preserving the figure's caption group.

The time-series example also checks that a single salmon-blue accent chart does
not look out of place next to the more categorical palette examples. That is the
kind of comparison a template needs to survive in ordinary manuscript drafting,
where figures rarely all share the same geometry.

This dummy paragraph gives the time-series chart a realistic delay after its
reference. A chart inserted in source order should still float to a page edge
when the text block is already partly filled. The point is not the data; the
point is the page behaviour.

The extra prose is intentionally separated from the chart chunk. This keeps
the remaining pages realistic without adding more table examples.

```{r}
#| label: fig-academic-air
#| chart-title: "Passenger counts rise sharply in the late 1950s"
#| chart-subtitle: "Monthly totals from the built-in AirPassengers series"
#| chart-notes: "The example is included to exercise a time-series chart in the same academic style."
#| chart-source: "R datasets package."
#| fig-width: 6.6
#| fig-height: 4.0
air_df |>
  ggplot(aes(year + (as.numeric(month) - 1) / 12, passengers)) +
  geom_line(colour = wfm_palette()[["blue"]], linewidth = 0.82) +
  geom_point(colour = wfm_palette()[["salmon"]], size = 1.25, alpha = 0.82) +
  scale_y_wfm() +
  labs(x = "Year", y = NULL, subtitle = "Passengers")
```

# Palette Checks

@fig-academic-palette is synthetic. It uses all seven colours in the
default palette order so that a single page can reveal whether the salmon, teal,
purple, lime, yellow, blue, and pink sequence remains legible in the formal
academic setting. The choice is intentionally softer than a strict
publication-first palette, but the example keeps the sequence explicit for
brand consistency and for comparison with colour-documentation guidance such as
@brewer2003colorbrewer.

The final chart is again separated from its reference by dummy text. It should
therefore make clear whether the remaining material is being handled as a float
queue. The bibliography barrier at the end of the document is retained only to
prevent a late float from drifting into the references.

```{r}
#| label: fig-academic-palette
#| chart-title: "The academic style keeps the wfmR palette order"
#| chart-subtitle: "Seven bars exercise every default categorical colour"
#| chart-notes: "The values are illustrative and are ordered only to show the default colour sequence."
#| chart-source: "Illustrative data."
#| fig-width: 6.6
#| fig-height: 4.0
category_df |>
  ggplot(aes(group, value, fill = group)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.72) +
  scale_fill_wfm() +
  scale_y_wfm(limits = c(0, NA)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, subtitle = "Value") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```
